text: 4.3 Database Design

A well-structured database is the backbone of any system design, since it is where all the information generated by the new process above needs to be stored, connected and retrieved efficiently. This section presents the objectives behind the proposed database, followed by an Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram and a data dictionary describing each table in detail.
4.3.1 Objectives

items: Efficient Data Store all information related to customers, sellers, products, orders, payments, deliveries, return and support tickets in a structured, non-repetitive way.

Support for New Trust and security Features: Provide dedicated fields for seller-trust scores, fraud risk scores,OTP verification status and delivery proof codes, so the new processes described in Section 4.2 have a proper place to store their data
Data integrity: use primary and foreign keys to make sure that every order, payment, delivery, return, and support ticket is correctly linked back to the right customer,seller and product.
Scalability: Design tables so that they can handle a very large number of daily orders and users without needing a major redesign as Daraz Bangladesh continues to grow.

Support for Reporting: Make it possible to easily generate reports such as “average refund time” or "average delivery dispute rate per seller” which are useful for monitoring whether the proposed system is actually working as intended.

text: 4.3.2 Entity Relationship (ER) Diagram
The Entity-Relationship diagram below shows the main tables (entities) in the proposed database, their key attributes, and how they connect to one another.

At the center of the design is the Order table, which connects to almost every other table: a Customer places one or more Orders, each Order contains one or more OrderItems drawn from the Product table, and each Order has exactly one Payment record and one Delivery record.An Order may also be linked to one or more ReturnRefund records if the customer requests a return, and to one or more SupportTicket records if the customer needs help. The Seller table connects to Product, since each product is listed by exactly one seller,and this is the table where the new seller Trust Score is stored.

text: 4.4 Form Design

This section presents wireframe designs for the key new or modified forms needed to support the proposed system. Unlike the existing forms discussed in Chapter 3 , which mostly already work well for ordinary orders, the forms below are new or meaningfully changed to directly support the new processes described in section 4.2.
4.4.1 Seller Verification Form

This form is completed by a new seller before their shop is allowed to go live. It supports process 2.0 from the proposed DFD, collecting identity and business information that feeds into the seller’s Trust Score.
Figure 4.3: Wireframe design of the proposed Seller Verification form

This form asks for the shop name, the owner’s full name and a National ID number,along with an uploaded photo of the ID itself. An optional trade license upload is available for sellers who have one, which can further increase their trust score once verified. A business category dropdown helps route the listing into the correct product category for later authenticity checks.
4.4.2 OTP / Account Security Verification Form

This form supports process 5.0, Fraud Detection and OTP Verification. It only appears when the system’s risk-scoring engine flags an activity as unusual, such as a login from a new device followed by a high-value order.
Figure 4.4: Wireframe design of the proposed OTP/Account security Verification form.

The form shows the customer’s registered mobile number and asks them to enter a six-digit one-time code sent by SMS. It also clearly displays the location and date of the activity that triggered this extra check, so the customer can immediately recognize whether this was really them. A clearly visible “This wasn’t me” option lets the customer instantly freeze their account if they did not request this login or purchase, directly addressing the account-security identified in Chapter 1.
4.4.3 Return / Refund Request Form

This form supports process 10.0, Return and Refund with Digital Receipt. It replaces the simpler existing return form discussed in Chapter 3 with one that immediately confirms the request with a trackable digital receipt.
Figure 4.5: Wireframe design of the proposed Return / Refund Request form.

The customer selects the order, chooses a reason for the return from a dropdown list and can optionally upload a photo if the product arrived damaged. Once submitted, the system immediately generates a Digital Return Receipt with its own tracking ID, directly solving the problem identified in Chapter 1 and Chapter 2, where customers were previously left without any confirmation that their return had been received.
4.4.4 Delivery Proof Capture Form(Rider App)
This form supports process 9.0, Deliver Order and Capture Proof. It is used by the delivery rider’s own app at the moment of delivery , not by the customer directly.
Figure 4.5: Wireframe design of the proposed Delivery proof Capture form of the Rider App.

At the point of delivery , the rider must enter the delivery OTP shown to the customer or capture a quick photo of the handover, before the order can be marked as delivered. If the customer is not available, the rider is required to log a call attempt along with a timestamp before the system will accept a “failed delivery” status. This directly addresses the delivery-dispute problem identified in Chapter 1, where deliveries were sometimes marked as failed without any way for the customer to verify what actually happened.
4.5 Conclusion

This Chapter has taken the problems and root causes identified in Chapter 1 through 3 and turned them into an actual system design. Two candidate systems were proposed and compared using both a qualitative comparison and a weighted scoring matrix and Candidate system 1, the more comprehensive,automated option,was selected as the recommended design.

A detailed Data Flow Diagram showed exactly how the new processes, seller verification, fraud detection, delivery proof capture, digital return receipts and support ticket escalation, fit into the existing order-to-delivery workflow. The database design, including the Entity-Relationship diagram and the full data dictionary, showed how this new information can be stored in a structured, connected way. Finally, four key form designs showed what these new processes would actually look like from the point of view of a seller, a customer and a delivery rider.

Together,these design elements form a complete and realistic answer to the problems first identified in Chapter 1 of this report. If implemented, this design would give Daraz Bangladesh stronger seller accountability, better fraud protection,clearer delivery accountability,faster and more transparent refunds and a more reliable customer support process, addressing the root causes identified throughout this report rather than only their surface symptoms.
